q: Take an examiner through why Alsace has more distinct soil types than any other French wine region, and how you would actually use that at a table.
accept: rhine graben rift faulting shattered the vosges edge into a soil mosaic
rift valley collapse exposed granite limestone sandstone schist and volcanic rock
vosges uplift and the rhine graben created thirteen major soil types
fault blocks from the rhine rift give the soil diversity granite for riesling limestone for gewurztraminer
ans: Alsace sits on the western shoulder of the Rhine Graben, the rift that collapsed some thirty-five to forty million years ago while the Vosges and the Black Forest were thrust up on either side of it. The collapse shattered that edge into a mosaic of fault blocks, so a few hundred metres of walking crosses granite and gneiss, Vosges pink sandstone, Muschelkalk and Jurassic limestone, marl, schist, and at Thann a volcanic sediment found nowhere else in the region — with loess and alluvial fans spread over the plain below. Thirteen major soil types is the figure usually quoted. At the table I use it predictively rather than decoratively: granite for tense, high-toned, quick-maturing Riesling, as at Schlossberg or Brand; limestone and marl-limestone for broad, structured, slow Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, as at Hengst or Goldert; schist for smoky austerity at Kastelberg; volcanic Rangen for gunflint and salt. Soil is the honest way to sell a grand cru whose name means nothing to the guest — it explains the wine in the glass rather than asserting a rank.
exp: The examiner is testing whether geology is vocabulary or a tool. The rift is the single cause behind every scattered fact about Alsace terroir — the soil mosaic, the steep west-bank slopes, the rain shadow and the sunshine hours all follow from the same tectonic event. Finish by mapping soil to style with named crus; a candidate who lists rock types without predicting a wine has recited a textbook, not answered the question.

q: You are poured a rich, off-dry aromatic white. Talk through how you separate Alsace Pinot Gris from Alsace Gewurztraminer, and then Alsace Riesling from German Riesling, out loud.
accept: gewurztraminer shows lychee and rose with low acid and phenolic bitterness pinot gris shows smoke and weight
pinot gris is weight over perfume gewurztraminer is overt rose and lychee
alcohol to sweetness ratio separates alsace from german riesling twelve to thirteen versus eight or nine
alsace riesling is drier and higher in alcohol mosel is lower alcohol higher acid and slaty
ans: Gewurztraminer announces itself: deep gold even when young, lychee, rose petal, ginger and allspice, low acidity, high alcohol at thirteen and a half to fifteen, an oily viscous palate and a bitter phenolic grip on the finish that comes from the pink skins. Pinot Gris is the quieter one — smoke, quince, ripe pear, honey, sometimes mushroom or toasted almond, and crucially more weight than aroma: the impact is on the mid-palate rather than the nose, acidity is fractionally higher, and residual sugar is often better hidden by the extract. If I cannot smell rose, and the wine is broad but not perfumed, I am on Pinot Gris. For the Riesling question I go first to alcohol and sweetness together, because that ratio is the border: an Alsace Riesling is twelve to thirteen and a half per cent and dry to just off-dry, with riper citrus and stone fruit, a phenolic grip and sometimes a whisper of botrytis; a Mosel Prädikat wine with comparable sweetness sits at eight or nine per cent, higher in acid, lighter in body, with slate and green apple and lime. The hard call is a German dry Grosses Gewächs, which matches Alsace on alcohol — there I lean on fruit register and texture: the German is tauter, higher in acid and more stony, the Alsatian riper, broader and more phenolic. Then I name my conclusion and the two facts that would change it.
exp: The deduction that fails at Master is the one that guesses the answer and then looks for support. The reliable structural markers here are alcohol against residual sugar, and phenolic bitterness on the finish — both of which come from something real: skin colour on Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, and the northern picking window in Germany. Note also that the 2021 sweetness-labelling reform helps only after you have committed; blind, the ratio is your only guide.

q: Describe how Alsace's wine business is actually structured — who grows, who makes, who sells — and what that means for a buyer.
accept: co-operatives take about a third of production ribeauville founded 1895 is the oldest in france
co-ops negociant houses and thousands of tiny growers with cremant as the volume engine
cremant is about a quarter of production and the co-ops' commercial engine
the label name is often the co-op or negociant so buy grower lieux-dits over the grand cru tier
ans: Three streams. First, the co-operatives, which handle roughly a third of the region's production and include Cave de Ribeauvillé, founded in 1895 and the oldest co-operative cellar in France, alongside Turckheim, Bestheim and Wolfberger. Second, the large négociant houses, which buy fruit and wine broadly and are the region's export face. Third, several thousand small growers whose holdings are measured in a handful of hectares split across many parcels, of whom only a minority bottle their own wine at all. Crémant d'Alsace is the engine underneath all of it — around a quarter of the region's volume and France's best-selling crémant — because it absorbs high-cropped fruit from the plain and pays reliably, which is exactly what a co-operative needs. For a buyer, three consequences. The price ladder is unusually flat, so grand cru fruit can end up in blended bottlings that never say so. The name on the label frequently is not the person who farmed the vineyard, so provenance questions matter more here than in Burgundy. And the genuine value sits in named lieux-dits from grower estates, which cost less than the grand cru tier and are often better farmed.
exp: Master orals ask about commerce because a sommelier buys as well as pours. Alsace's flat price ladder is the root of several other problems the region complains about — it removes the financial reward for lower yields, which is why the 55 hl/ha grand cru ceiling has never been tightened. Know at least one co-operative by name and one thing it does well: Ribeauvillé for its history, Turckheim for the quality of its grand cru cuvées.

q: Alsace has spent years trying to insert a Premier Cru tier between AOC Alsace and Grand Cru. Make the case for it, then say what stands in the way.
accept: premier cru would give legal standing to the lieux-dits already being bottled
the obstacle is agreeing which sites qualify because boundaries are land value
a third tier risks making an already crowded alsace label less legible
inao accepted the principle in 2022 and the lieux-dit assessment continues
ans: The case is that the real quality signal in Alsace already exists and has no legal standing. Hundreds of named lieux-dits are bottled every year by serious growers with nothing behind the name, while the tier above them is over-broad: fifty-one crus, some of them large and internally uneven, a base yield of fifty-five hectolitres, and a boycott by two of the region's most famous houses. A premier cru rung would give the good non-grand-cru sites recognition, restore a hierarchy a Burgundy-literate customer can read, and shift the market's attention from variety to place, which is the region's stated ambition. Against it: deciding which lieux-dits qualify and where the lines fall is a land-value fight in which every grower is an interested party, and Alsace has already shown it settles such fights by including people. A third tier also risks making a label that already carries variety, village, lieu-dit, sweetness indication and possibly grand cru less legible rather than more. And the deepest objection is that the grand cru tier's problem was never a missing rung — it was enforcement and credibility, neither of which a new category fixes. The INAO accepted the principle in 2022 and the site-by-site assessment has continued since; I would date any status claim I make.
exp: This is a judgement question, not a recall one — the examiner wants to hear you argue both sides and then place yourself. The historical warning is built in: the grand cru tier grew from one site in 1975 to fifty-one, which is what happens when a classification is negotiated among the people being classified. Say plainly that regulatory status moves, and date your information rather than asserting a fixed present.
